articles.title: Pakistan export initiative
articles.content: DOES any such initiative exist in our country, or is it a figment of my imagination? For sure, there is an initiative for remittances — but not for exports. One wonders about the presence of one and the strange absence of the other. Exports are stagnating, andremittances are rising. Are exports falling because of unwise policies or despite them? Are remittances rising because of good policy initiatives or despite them? The point here is not to denigrate the remittances initiative or its continually renewed push, but to emphasise that exports should be given greater policy priority than remittances — because, in some growth-promoting way, exports matter far more than remittances. Here we explore the reasons. This article focuses on increasing exports, not reducing remittances. In fact, remittances should continue to be promoted. Both exports and remittances matter to our economy. Both help contain the current account deficit. Exports are driven by agricultural, industrial, and services output — sectors that already provide a direct impetus to employment in the country. This impetus also has an indirect impact on the economy through spending by household members employed in export industries. Remittances follow increased output in foreign countries that employ Pakistani workers and pay them abroad. Part of their overseas earnings/ savings is sent home to their families. The economic impact of remittances is indirect and arises from spending by remittance-receiving families. Hence, both help fill the gap in the current account, but the growth impact of exports is both direct and indirect, while it is only indirect for remittances. Another, far more crucial point is that increasing exports to raise the economy’s productivity is paramount for growth. This is not true for rising remittances in Pakistan, although it is theoretically possible if a larger proportion of remittances goes towards export production. Our policymakers seem to have forgotten the importance of exports. A policy to increase exports is more likely to raise productivity than a policy to increase remittances. Increased productivity can fuel long-term sustainable growth. Exporting exposes domestic firms to international competition, better management practices, international quality standards, global supply chains, and new technologies. There is considerable empirical evidence that exporters tend to be more productive and that export expansion can generate productivity gains. For example, the World Bank reports that a 10 per cent increase in exports across its cross-country sample was associated with higher employment, earnings, and productivity. Another point to note is that exports are always preceded by the actual rise in production and employment (direct impact), as well as the indirect impact through consumption made possible by spending of wages by export-related employees. Contrast this with remittances, whose economic impact is not only indirect but also follows the receipt of remittances. This means that prioritising sustained export growth would create more employment in the country and reduce the desperation of unemployed people pushed abroad to find jobs, even at the risk of their lives. At the same time, increasing exports would have boosted the productivity our economy so badly needs. This is why remittances should not be seen as a substitute for exports. Exports should be promoted with more vigour than remittances. In terms of promoting growth, exports matter far more than remittances. Our analysts tend to blame high unemployment almost entirely on high population growth. The fact is that our unwise economic policies are at the root of frequent economic crises that cause growth and productivity to decline. The resulting rise in joblessness leads to greater migration abroad, which, in turn, drives remittances up. Of course, Pakistan’s remittance initiative has helped. But if we had implemented prudent policies that avoided various crises, exports as a proportion of GDP would have risen much faster than remittances. The export-to-GDP ratio peaked at 17.3pc in 1992 (according to World Bank data). It went down to only 10pc of GDP in 2025. The trajectory of the fall was not linear. Every onslaught of a balance-of-payments crisis precipitated a large decline. It fell to 9.6pc of GDP in 2000 in the wake of the 1998-99 crisis. With more prudent policies after the crisis, it recovered somewhat — only to decline again when imprudent policies followed, leading to other crises between 2000 and now. In contrast, our remittances have been rising almost consistently during this period as a proportion of GDP. Remittances dipped from 3.2pc of GDP in 1992 to 1.1pc of GDP in 2000, then rose to 9.9pc. The presence of a falling trend in exports and a rising trend in remittances indicates that exports always respond positively to prudent economic policies, while remittances largely show autonomous growth. Refinements in the banking infrastructure have indeed helped to increase remittances, but economic policies also played a role that pushed people into boats to find employment abroad. Subsequent remittance growth has largely occurred despite these economic policies. Pakistan’s export potential is much higher than its current level suggests. The simplest way to estimate what the level of exports could have been in 2026 is to assume the export-to-GDP ratio of 1992 (17.3pc). This translates to exports valued at $78bn, compared with the actual export value of $41bn (FY26 State Bank data). Frequent balance-of-payments crises in our country seem to have clouded the thinking of our policymakers. When they think about exports or remittances or even foreign investment, they only think in terms of foreign exchange earnings or inflows that fill a gap in the balance-of-payments. Constant firefighting and pressing short- and mid-term foreign financing needs have created a policy psyche that is obsessed with mobilising foreign exchange liquidity and has forgotten productivity and growth. Exports are badly in need of an initiative based on collective policy expertise in the country. The writer is a former deputy governor of the State Bank of Pakistan.
articles.author: Riaz Riazuddin

articles.title: Decoding defence deals
articles.content: SINCE September 2025, Pakistan has signed multilayered and multi-domain defence agreements with several Arab and Muslim states. It has signed aStrategic Mutual Defence Agreement(SMDA) with Saudi Arabia, theMakkah Joint Defence Agreement(MJDA) with Turkiye and Saudi Arabia, and a defence pact with Kuwait. Pakistan has recently signed another defence agreement — theBadr agreement. Pakistan, Turkiye, Qatar, and Indonesia are signatories to this pact. These defence deals have, in the past year, increased Pakistan’s strategic relevance in the Middle East. Interestingly, each accord carries the explicit provision for joint defence production and investment in the defence industry. This clause in every defence pact reveals Islamabad’s long-term strategic objective of moving from a buyer-seller relationship to a co-production partnership with reliable partners in the region. There are four primary strategic factors that have driven Islamabad’s emphasis on the joint defence production clause in each defence pact. The India factor remains the primary driver. New Delhi’s defence budget now exceeds $80 billion, and its rapid induction of advanced platforms has widened the qualitative gap. Joint production arrangements with middle powers are likely to allow Pakistan to accelerate defence modernisation without bearing the full research and development cost. By manufacturing components and subsystems domestically, Pakistan can sustain a higher operational tempo and maintain credible conventional deterrence. Islamabad believes that strategic parity in South Asia does not require numerical equivalence. It primarily requires the ability to absorb, adapt, and indigenise technology at a pace that may prevent New Delhi from achieving decisive superiority over Islamabad. These defence deals, therefore, function as a force-multiplier for Pakistan’s conventional and strategic capabilities. Pakistan’s defence pacts over the past year have increased its strategic relevance. Islamabad’s second strategic objective is the diversification of defence suppliers and reduced reliance of its defence supply chain on Western weapons. Historically, Islamabad has relied on Chinese weapons but the extent of dependency has increased significantly in the last two decades. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute has noted that this dependency is nearly 80 per cent. Although Pakistan and China enjoy unprecedented trust and depth in their all-weather strategic relationship, in theoretical terms, heavy reliance on any single external source worries Islamabad. Similarly, Islamabad is increasingly seeking to decouple its military procurement from Western-reliant supply chains. This approach is rooted in Pakistan’s historically bitter experiences with sudden embargoes and sanctions, alongside Islamabad’s broader resistance to the West’s tendency to use defence exports as political leverage over the Global South during geopolitical crises. Primarily, Islamabad is eager to cultivate robust, non-Western defence partnerships to secure reliable and uninterrupted arms supplies free from the influence of foreign powers. By integrating affluent Saudi and Qatari capital with the technologically advanced Turkish weapons industry, Pakistan is building an insulated, collaborative defence network with the middle powers to achieve this strategic objective. Islamabad believes that these defence deals, alongside its strategic alliance with China, may allow Islamabad to minimise its conventional vulnerabilities, help modernise its armed forces, and ultimately achieve a much higher degree of long-term strategic autonomy. Moreover, Islamabad is acutely aware that the intensifying US-China strategic competition will make it increasingly difficult to maintain a purely China-centric defence supply chain in the long run. Therefore, by building parallel defence production partnerships with Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Turkiye, and Indonesia, Pakistan is creating a middle-power buffer to avoid unwanted political pressure from the US. Interestingly, these countries are not fully aligned with either Washington or Beijing, and provide Islamabad greater room for manoeuvre. Third, the economic factor equally occupies the strategic motivations of Islamabad. Pakistan wants to enhance its ability to modernise the defence production industry and increase defence exports. Pakistan’s official defence exports stood at approximately $280m in 2024. The recently concluded deals can significantly enhance defence exports to $650-700m by 2027, crossing the $1bn mark by 2030. The Gulf states, seeking to reduce their own dependence on Western suppliers, constitute the most immediate and lucrative market for Pakistani defence exports. Joint ventures under the Badr agreement, MJDA and SMDA are designed to produce systems that meet the Gulf’s operational requirements, while carrying Pakistani certification, and, crucially, a lower price tag. Successful penetration of these markets would generate much-needed foreign exchange for Pakistan, create skilled employment, and justify further capital investment in the domestic defence industry. Beyond the Gulf, there is also potential for niche exports to African and Central Asian countries that face similar budgetary constraints and seek cost-effective, reliable platforms. The fourth objective linked to the third is to attract foreign direct investment to Pakistan’s defence sector. The joint production clauses are structured to encourage equity participation rather than simple technology licensing. Early commitments already indicate potential inflows of $1.2-1.5bn over the next five years in manufacturing facilities, testing ranges, and human capital development. These investments will upgrade the physical infrastructure of Pakistan’s public-sector defence industry. These inflows can stimulate related industries, including electronics, metallurgy, and software, while creating thousands of high-skill jobs for individuals who would otherwise migrate overseas. Time will tell whether these defence deals can deliver a meaningful technology transfer. The most important question is whether such a multipronged approach can genuinely enhance Pakistan’s long-term strategic autonomy or will merely redistribute its dependencies. It is also unclear to what extent these defence deals can genuinely reduce Pakistan’s strategic vulnerabilities. However, despite these uncertainties, these defence deals will bring critical capital and technical know-how, while reducing vulnerability to external supply shocks. Yet Islamabad must calibrate its exposure with precision. Over-commitment in the complex security theatres of the Middle East can risk entangling Pakistan in conflicts whose political and military logic lies beyond Islamabad’s core interests. Therefore, Pakistan must pursue these opportunities with strategic clarity and within well-defined red lines. The writer is a strategic analyst of international security. The views expressed are his own.
articles.author: Khurram Abbas

articles.title: The next Waseem
articles.content: I HAVE eight columns left to write this year after this one. I said the last two months should be different. Cheerful maybe. Insightful, at least. Something new. Then Waseem Abbas happened. He was 15. His father died nine years ago. His mother remarried. A grandfather and an uncle took turns looking after him until they could not. Then they took him to an orphanage in Multan. His grandfather said he wanted the boy to get an education rather than struggle on the streets. That was five years ago. Waseem wanted to learn electrical work. The orphanage sent him to a contractor, Tauqeer Nazir, after what it says were inquiries. Media reports say Tauqeer had a team of around 40 boys. Six days later, Waseem was dead. According to the FIR, he ran. He passed residents on a street in a private housing society and told them the men behind him wanted to kill him. A car followed. His head struck a pillar at a gate. His skull was crushed. His cousin says Waseem had often said he did not want to go to the electrician. He wanted to go home. He was buried at 2am in Muzaffargarh. Only close relatives and orphanage officials attended. Arrest, escape, encounter, closure. We know the sequence well. Tauqeer was arrested at the scene. Lawyers beat him outside the courtroom, though police were present. A magistrate gave him four days of physical remand. That night, according to the Crime Control Department, he escaped. By the next morning, he was dead, killed in an exchange of fire near Bahawalpur. His accomplice, the CCD says, got away. Many of us cheered. I understand why. A boy was crushed against a gate, and the man accused of doing it is gone. It feels like the scales have been balanced. But I have read this story before. So have you. Arrest, escape, encounter, closure. We know the sequence well enough to recite it. We know what it says about our policing, and about courts that many people no longer trust to deliver. None of this is a secret. Last year, the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan counted more than 500 alleged encounters in Punjab since January 2025, with over 670 people killed — more than in any other province. It said the killings had become normal since the CCD was set up in February 2025, and that encounters were standing in for the criminal justice system. The CCD rejected the allegations, saying it works within the law and that hardened criminals often fire first. The statement made the news for a day. Then we moved on. Now some of us applaud. Among them was lawmaker Hina Parvez Butt who tweeted that justice was served immediately. She later deleted it and said it was the feelings of an ordinary citizen. That is precisely the problem. When an elected representative mistakes the killing of a suspect for justice, what hope is there for the ordinary citizen? So, I have nothing new to say about the encounter, except perhaps this: a trial would have belonged to Waseem. It would have asked questions in public and on the record. Why did a 15-year-old run from the man teaching him a trade? What happened in the six days before? Who is Amjad Ali, the second man named in the FIR, and where is he now? What did the orphanage ask before sending the child away? What happens to the other boys who worked for Tauqeer? Those questions now have no courtroom. The case against Tauqeer appears to have been closed. The case for Waseem never opened. Our institutions are often at their most energetic after a funeral. A licence is reviewed — in this case the orphanage’s. A statement is posted. A file is closed, sometimes with a bullet. What we rarely build is the dull machinery that would have made the funeral unnecessary. A register. An inspection. A phone number that a frightened boy could dial. Most of us reading this are lucky. When our children turn 15, learning a trade means an internship arranged by a family friend. Someone checks on them. If they hate it, they come home and complain at dinner. Nobody chases them down a street. Waseem had a cousin who listened and a grandfather who hoped. What he did not have was a system. Somewhere this week another boy is being placed with someone to learn a trade. He may be lucky. The contractor may be kind. But if he is not, and he runs, who will he run to? I promised myself something hopeful, so here is the most hopeful thing I can find. An old man in Muzaffargarh took his grandson to an orphanage because he believed there was a better life on the other side of its gate. That belief should not be naive. The writer is a journalist and conducts writing workshops in Karachi.
articles.author: Muna Khan

articles.title: Pak-US reset?
articles.content: SINCE early 2025, Pakistan’s relations with the US have taken an upturn after years of mutual disenchantment. Why did the US opt for this reset? And will this bonhomie last? Historically, Pakistan and the US have come close only when their interests converged. America has preferred a transactional relationship with Pakistan based on specific issues of its geopolitical agenda. The recent thaw in ties can, therefore, be better understood in terms of how global geopolitics is evolving. It is no longer a unipolar world led by the US. Since the dawn of this century, several centres of power have arisen while the US remains entangled in long, distant wars. The US reliance on its military might to subdue adversaries has taken a heavy toll on America’s world standing. Into this evolving geometry of global power politics stepped Donald Trump, who has ruptured the trans-Atlantic alliance, pulled back support for Ukraine in its war against Russia, and sought to stabilise America’s ties with China. However, nothing has compromised America’s domestic and international standing more than the recent US-Iran war. As for Pakistan-US ties, three developments seem to have contributed to the recent thaw. First is Pakistan’s role in countering terrorism. In March 2025, President Trump thanked Pakistan in his State of the Union address to Congress for apprehending the mastermind of a bombing in Kabul on the eve of the US exit from Afghanistan. Later, Centcom chief Gen Michael Kurilla described Pakistan to Congress as a “phenomenal partner in the world of counterterrorism”. In June 2025, Trump hosted Pakistan’s army chief for lunch at the White House. And in August, BLA was designated as a terrorist organisation by the US. Three developments seem to have contributed to the recent thaw. Second, the US, like the rest of the world, saw Pakistan robustly counter Indian aggression in May 2025. The US mediated a ceasefire on May 10. Pakistan acknowledged America’s positive role. New Delhi, on the other hand, was reluctant to acknowledge Trump’s role, even though India itself had asked the US to secure a ceasefire. Third, Pakistan’s mediatory role in the recent US-Iran conflict has convinced Washington of Pakistan’s important role as a net stability provider in the region. Meanwhile, America’s distrust of India has deepened because the latter has bought Russian oil while ignoring US sanctions, and has maintained continued economic ties with China while pretending to be a US partner to counterbalance China. America is no longer convinced that India can be a trustworthy counterweight to China. How will this reset impact Pakistan’s other key relationship? Islamabad’s close ties with Beijing are not unknown to Washington. The Chinese leadership is also well aware of the strategic nature of Sino-Pak relations. In an era where cooperation and confrontation coexist, Pakistan has ample space to pursue mutually beneficial relations with both China and the US based on its own national interest. India is upset at the uptick in Pakistan’s ties with the US, and its own failure to isolate Pakistan diplomatically. As for Afghanistan, the US has not shown any interest in it, even as the country is on the cusp of becoming a safe haven for world terrorists. The US is also aware of the fine balance that Pakistan has always maintained in its ties with both Iran and Saudi Arabia. How should Pakistan use this reset in its relationship with the US, even if it was transactional, for mutual benefit? Several promising areas can be identified: Pakistan must ensure that its share of flourishing trade with the US is maintained and enhanced. The US offers bright prospects for Pakistan’s young, tech-savvy entrepreneurs, IT exports, startups, software development, growing digital adop- tion, and e-commerce. American companies should be encouraged to invest in Pakistan’s shale oil potential and minerals sector, especially lithium, rare earth elements, and copper — crucial for the semiconductor industry, defence technology and robotics, among others. Other promising areas of cooperation include defence, security, and counterterrorism. Agriculture has been a legacy area of cooperation since the 1950s, as have education and public health. However, all this will only be possible if Pakistan addresses its policy and regulatory hurdles, cost of doing business, security risks, and infrastructure issues. Today’s Pakistan stands tall as a competent, self-confident power that can contribute to regional peace, stability, and development. However, this window of opportunity may be limited because global geopolitics is constantly evolving. What matters most is making the best use of the recent thaw in Pakistan-US ties while preserving our other key relationships, including with China. The writer is a former ambassador to the US and is currently serving as chairman of the Sanober Institute.
articles.author: Aizaz Ahmad Chaudhry

articles.title: Prudent warning
articles.content: AS speculation grows regarding fresh US-Israeli aggression against Iran, major Muslim states of the wider Middle East, as well as European powers, have clearly expressed their lack of appetite for any such misadventure. Meeting in Istanbul on Friday under the ‘R4+E3’ umbrella, the foreign ministers of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Turkiye, the UK, Germany, and Francediscussedseveral global hotspots, including Iran and Ukraine. Italy also participated in the meeting. The Turkish foreign minister said that “no one supports” military intervention in Iran at this moment, while France’s top diplomat said any escalation “would only have losers”, besides increasing oil prices, which are already high. There is good reason for the international community to be worried. Strong signals are emerging from Tel Aviv and Washington that the US and Israel are planning a new assault on Iran, reportedly after the American midterms on Nov 3 — perhaps even earlier. US President Donald Trump has himself said that “we may do another little Epic Fury”, referring to the name America gave to the aggression launched in February. While the US leader is known for his bluster and often non-serious threats, in this regard he may actually mean what he has said. The US has been sending more troops and military equipment to the Middle East, and American and Israeli forces have reportedly rehearsed attack plans. Tel Aviv is particularly enthused about going after Iran again. Doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results each time is equated with folly. But arrogance has blinded both the US and Israel to this reality. Israel had firstattackedIran in October 2024, while both the US and the Zionist state initiated two more aggressive operations against the Islamic Republic, in June 2025 and February 2026. These attacks, particularly the assault launched this year, inflicted huge damage on Iran, decimating its military, political, and religious leadership. But the country regrouped, defended itself, and fought back against the aggressors. The Iranians have reaffirmed that any new attack will be met with “offensive” measures. All of this is cause for alarm. The Gulf states that host American facilities will again be in the line of fire, which is why Muslim countries have warned against a new conflict. But will the war lobbies in Washington and Tel Aviv listen? Many governments and most people of the Middle East are tired of war, and want to rebuild their lives and economies. If conflict and bloodshed return, the shockwaves caused by disrupted energy and trade flows will leave few economies unscathed. Therefore, America should abandon its plans to further destabilise the region. Instead, it should rein in its ally Israel and its bloodthirsty leaders.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Party of one
articles.content: IT ill behoves a political party that claims to be the biggest and most popular in the country to be so mired in chaos all the time. Yet it sometimes appears as if this is exactly what its leader intended. At each turning point in national politics since the PTI’s founder was jailed, the party has demonstrated a lack of capacity to function rationally. Former prime minister Imran Khan, while he still had access to his party cadres, routinely vetoed any course of action that could risk weakening his hand. But the government’s decision to cut off that access did not help either. Over the last year, the government has tried to compel the remaining PTI leadership to make major choices on the party’s behalf independently. Here, the PTI’s lack of internal discipline has prevented it from acting as a reasonable, reliable counterparty for negotiation and dialogue. The last-minute breakdown of recent talks between the government and opposition, which preceded the imposition of governor’s rule in KP, is a prime example. The government later blamed the PTI for changing its demands until the eleventh hour. This week alone, a senior office-bearer resigned, only to be persuaded to reconsider, and a senator quit the party’s WhatsApp groups after a row with its leadership. There is a certain calculation in how the PTI has been shaped. No one but Mr Khan can lead it. This is at once the party’s Achilles’ heel and the strongest guarantee that the former prime minister remains the only figure who can hold meaningful negotiations with the government. The government has not realised this. Meanwhile, by using state power to suppress the party, it has also strengthened the PTI’s victimhood narrative. That approach is not merely counterproductive, it is wrong in principle: a mainstream party cannot be wished away through arrests and legal manoeuvres, and each such attempt erodes the democratic space on which the government itself depends. Regrettably, the government has also struggled to counter the appeal of the PTI’s narrative by offering a better alternative, either through better policymaking or improved management of the economy. The citizenry, meanwhile, is stuck between the two: an opposition whose own leadership will not let it function, and a government that seems bereft of ideas and is adrift amid the challenges it faces. The breakthrough is still far away.
articles.author: Editorial
